name: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone

lead: TRH is a three-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus. It signals the pituitary to release TSH and prolactin, which control the thyroid, so it sits at the top of the thyroid axis that sets metabolism and energy. Hormone-minded readers discuss it for thyroid, mood and energy effects.

TRH binds receptors on pituitary thyrotroph cells and is cleared within minutes; in the brain it influences arousal and neurotransmitter release. Its discoverers shared the 1977 Nobel Prize, and clinical use has been mainly diagnostic, with human studies for other conditions small or dated.

paras: Clinically it is used as a diagnostic test of the thyroid axis. In peptide lists it appears in the recovery category because of brain effects seen in research.

Reported effects of injected TRH include nausea, flushing and a mild blood pressure rise. Because it raises TSH and prolactin, endocrine effects are expected, and it has not been established as a treatment for the conditions studied.

angle.text: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone sits at the top of the thyroid axis: it signals the pituitary to release TSH, raising thyroid activity that shapes metabolism and energy. Hormone-minded readers discuss it for thyroid, mood and energy effects; human studies outside diagnostics are small and dated.

lead: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH, also thyroliberin; the pharmaceutical form is protirelin) is a tripeptide, pyroglutamyl-histidyl-proline amide, made mainly by neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus. It stimulates the pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and prolactin, and so sits at the top of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.[1][2]

TRH was the first hypothalamic releasing hormone to be structurally identified, in 1969, and its discoverers shared the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[1] Beyond its endocrine role it acts in the brain, where it has been studied for effects on wakefulness, seizures, mood and neurological disease.[1] Clinical use has been mainly diagnostic, and trials of TRH for other conditions have been small or inconclusive. No source reviewed documents an established appearance-related use.

paras: TRH is cleaved from a larger precursor protein, and its pyroglutamyl and amidated ends protect it from some peptidases. It is rapidly degraded in blood, with a half-life of roughly five to six minutes.[1][2] Released into the portal circulation of the pituitary, it binds G protein-coupled receptors on thyrotroph cells, prompting TSH release, which in turn drives thyroid hormone production; thyroid hormones feed back to restrain TRH.[1][2]

TRH and its receptors also occur elsewhere in the nervous system and gut. Experimental work reports that TRH excites histamine-producing neurons that regulate arousal, and that it modulates glutamate release in brain tissue.[3]

The TRH stimulation test was historically used to distinguish hypothalamic from pituitary causes of hypothyroidism, a role largely replaced by ultrasensitive TSH assays.[1] Wikipedia also notes use in Japan-style indications such as spinocerebellar degeneration and disturbances of consciousness, and research interest in epilepsy, central nervous system injury and depression.[1]
Animal work has tested delivery methods intended to prolong TRH's brief action in the brain, including nanoparticles and implantable polymer discs, in seizure models.[4][5]

Wikipedia lists nausea, flushing, urinary urgency and a mild rise in blood pressure after intravenous administration, and tremor, sweating, shivering and restlessness after intrathecal administration.[1] A double-blind study in depressed alcoholic men reported mild and infrequent subjective side effects and no cardiovascular effects.[6]

Human studies of TRH are mostly old and small. A 1979 double-blind, placebo-controlled study in depressed alcoholic men found a beneficial behavioural effect three hours after injection, but not on later days.[6] A 1979 study of 17 schizophrenic patients reported a prompt decrease in psychotic symptoms of about half after intravenous protirelin, which then tended to fade.[7] A preliminary report examined TRH for spinal muscular atrophy, and Wikipedia states efficacy in ALS and spinal muscular atrophy has not been shown.[8][1]

Registered trials include large antenatal TRH studies for preventing respiratory distress in preterm infants (NCT00004778, Phase 3, 1,090 participants; NCT00004840, 996 participants), a Phase 2 trial for cancer-related fatigue that was terminated (NCT00790296), and Phase 2 trials of a TRH analogue coded KPS-0373 in spinocerebellar degeneration.[9][10][11][12]
